searches.note: Twenty five searches of a share of twenty eight, three left unspent, none of them the author's. Two were shared: the IPONZ register for Bannockburn (Mt Difficulty and the Felton Road label) and New Zealand Winegrowers' own pages on the sub-regions (Gibbston, Bendigo, Wanaka, Bannockburn), restricted to its domains. One was restricted to the house's domain (Rippon's history) and one to the host of Mt Difficulty's sheets, which returned nothing of the house; the others kept the house's own domain out where the author had leant on it, so that each second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail stood in only one page that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less; the house's own claims are told as its account.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, a critic's blog on Rippon, a Gibbston founder page whose address names him) are cited neither in the fragment nor here. Pages whose addresses name a living person (New Zealand Winegrowers' people pages for two founders, a winemaker profile, a feature on Felton Road's owner) were read in summaries and not cited.
The serving temperatures, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius for every record, agree with the service reference for medium reds; no air is promised to soften tannin.

tested: The founding of 1991, the first vines of 1992, Block 5 of 1993, the first vintage of 1997 and the sale of 2000: confirmed by the Sommelier Academy profile, Winestar and The Grape Reset with the house domain kept out; the founder researched the site in 1991 and planted in 1992. Sound.
Block 5 lies on a gentle north facing slope at the heart of The Elms (two merchants quoting the house). The record said only a north facing slope; set right.

The making: about a fifth whole bunch (a quarter in 2010), destemmed by gravity, a soak of eight to ten days, indigenous yeasts, twenty one to twenty five days on skins, sixteen to seventeen months in French oak, a quarter to a third or so new, unfined and unfiltered (House of Townend, Skurnik, Canterbury Wines, all with the house domain kept out). Sound.

The winemaker of 1997 as the founder's laboratory partner at Lincoln: one secondary calls them Lincoln contemporaries or classmates, none a laboratory partner; New Zealand Winegrowers alone says laboratory partner. Said with less.
Demeter certification (2010 in two accounts) and BioGro (2020 in one): both certifiers stand, without years. Sound.
Bannockburn on the south bank of the Kawarau, by New Zealand Winegrowers: the label line had set The Elms on the sluicings themselves; set right.
Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanation teaches. Rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: In 1990, by New Zealand Winegrowers' account, Felton Road's founder enrolled in the viticulture course at Lincoln University, and in 1991, the year the house dates its beginning to, he chose and laid out a vineyard just off Felton Road at Bannockburn, a district of old gold sluicings above the Kawarau. The first vines went in in 1992, and Block 5 followed in 1993 in what became The Elms Vineyard. In 1997 a young winemaker who had been the founder's laboratory partner at Lincoln made the first official Felton Road Pinot Noir, and in 2000 the founder sold the estate to a British wine lover. The house came to bottle the blocks of The Elms apart, Block 3 and Block 5 above all, and to farm its vineyards biodynamically, certified by Demeter and by BioGro, with wild yeasts in the cellar and no fining or filtering before bottling. Block 5's soils run from loess and silt to clay and schist gravel, with old lake bed sediments at its heart, and its wine is the darker and spicier of the two. For a sommelier the pair is a lesson in how far soil alone can move Pinot Noir within one vineyard.

tested: The family's land since 1912: the house says the Mills family has farmed it for four generations from 1912, and that Wanaka Station was bought by the founder's grandfather; one secondary dates his purchase to 1912. The record now says the founder's family and the grandfather, by its own account.
The war: the founder served in submarines in the Second World War (the house, RNZ, the Otago Daily Times); no source read gives him the rank of lieutenant. Said with less.

The move home in 1973, the trial of some thirty varieties in 1975 and the first commercial block of 1982 against the doubts of the DSIR and other experts: the house's history. Two secondaries give 1974 for the first vines; the house's 1975 stands as its account.

The founding presidency: one secondary has him founding president of the region's winegrowers' association; the association's name in the record (Central Otago Grape Growers Association) was in no source read. Said without the name.

Mature Vine: two winters in barrel, fifteen to twenty per cent new in the first and none in the second, two years in bottle, unfined and unfiltered, hand picked and wild fermented (Berry Bros and Rudd, Wine.com, Caro's, the New Zealand Wine Catalogue). The share of whole bunches the record claimed was in no source read; cut.

Jeunesse Young Vine Pinot Noir: the house's Pinot Noir of its younger parcels, in Prince of Pinot, United Cellars and Delectable (a search of its own); added to others, which also explains Mature Vine.
Tinker's Field as the oldest vines on the property: two Lea and Sandeman pages and another listing. Sound.

The site: a north facing escarpment where terminal moraines meet an ancient cone of coarse schist gravels on the western edge of Roy's Bay (the house). The record's all of schist went further; set right.

Wanaka as the northernmost sub-region, moderated by the lake: New Zealand Winegrowers places Wanaka some eighty kilometres north of Queenstown and calls it cooler and slightly wetter, but no page read calls it the northernmost or says the lake moderates it. The label term keeps Lake Wanaka, which the trade copies from the labels (Jeunesse Young Vine Lake Wanaka Pinot Noir, Mature Vines Wanaka Pinot Noir), with a plainer meaning, and the trap is rewritten.

changed.was: The Mills family has farmed the land at Roy's Bay on Lake Wanaka since 1912, by its own account. The founder had thought of growing grapes there since coming home from the Second World War, in which he served as a submarine lieutenant, and in 1973 he and his wife moved back to the family farm. In 1975 he planted a trial of some thirty grape varieties beside the lake, among the first vines of modern Central Otago, and in 1982, against the doubts of research bodies and local experts, he planted the first commercial block, the year from which the house dates its winegrowing. He became the first president of the Central Otago Grape Growers Association, the forerunner of the region's winegrowers' association. After his death his widow carried on the business they had founded, and their son went on to lead the vineyard and the cellar. The estate is farmed biodynamically, and Mature Vine gathers all of its fully grown Pinot Noir, while two single blocks, Tinker's Field and Emma's Block, are bottled apart. For a sommelier, Rippon carries the modern region's story back to its trials of the 1970s: Pinot Noir from a lakeside farm where the vines began as an experiment.
changed.now: By its own account the founder's family has farmed the land at Roy's Bay on Lake Wanaka since 1912, part of the Wanaka Station his grandfather had bought. The founder had thought of growing grapes there since the Second World War, in which he served in submarines, and in 1973 he and his wife moved back to the family farm. In 1975 he planted a trial of some thirty grape varieties beside the lake, among the first vines of modern Central Otago, and in 1982, against the doubts of research bodies and local experts, he planted the first commercial block, the year from which the house dates its winegrowing. He became the founding president of the region's winegrowers' association. After his death his widow carried on the business they had founded, and their son went on to lead the vineyard and the cellar. The estate is farmed biodynamically. Mature Vine gathers all of its fully grown Pinot Noir and Jeunesse the younger vines, while two single blocks, Tinker's Field and Emma's Block, are bottled apart. For a sommelier, Rippon carries the modern region's story back to its trials of the 1970s: Pinot Noir from a lakeside farm where the vines began as an experiment.
changed.why: The house dates the family's farming to 1912 and the station's purchase to the founder's grandfather; no source gives the rank of lieutenant; the association's name in the record was in none; and Jeunesse takes the younger vines.

changed.was: Gibbston lies in the Kawarau Gorge between Queenstown and Cromwell, the highest and coolest corner of Central Otago. The house's founder planted his first vines there in the early 1980s, and in 1983, by the house's account, he planted its first commercial vineyard, the Home Block. In 1987 Gibbston Valley released the region's first commercial vintage, a date New Zealand Winegrowers gives for Gibbston's first commercial bottling. In 1990 the founder established Gibbston Valley Wines as a boutique winery with a tasting room and a restaurant, and by 1995 the barrels had outgrown their store; rather than build another, he had a cave blasted into the schist mountainside behind the winery, New Zealand's largest wine cave by the house's own account. The house came to grow at Bendigo too, on the warmer terraces by Lake Dunstan, where China Terrace and School House give its single vineyard wines. The Reserve is its selection of a few rows in a strong year, and the Reserve Pinot Noir of 2000 won the Pinot Noir trophy at the International Wine Challenge in London. For a sommelier the Reserve carries the region's early history: the first commercial vintage, the cave and a London trophy.

tested: The first vintage of 1998: The Real Review and others besides the author's Otago Daily Times. Sound.

The founding: a handshake among the owners of four new Bannockburn vineyards dated 1992 in one account, five owners in another, the first vintage 1998, the company 2004 in most accounts and 2003 in one. No founding year is sure, so founded is now empty.
The Gang of Four: two accounts call the group so; that they named themselves so is in none. Said as came to be known.
The company of 2004: most of the individual vineyards passed into it (one account). The record's the founding vineyards came into it went further; set right.

The clones 5, 6 and 10/5: found in no source of two searches, one of them restricted to the host of the house's sheets; a Pipeclay Terrace note of 2009 lists clones 5, 6, 13, 113, 115, 667 and 777. Cut to a blend of several clones.

The making: about twelve months on full lees in barrel, malolactic in spring, filtered but not fined (the house's 2016 sheet on another host, a 2024 merchant); ten months with a fifth new and a tenth whole bunch in 2021 (the Wine Advocate through Wine.com); twelve months with a fifth new and a fifth whole bunch in 2022 (two merchants). Rewritten with the bunches and the new oak.

Pipeclay Terrace: vines of 1996 on coarse, drought prone Bannockburn soils and heavy Scotland Point clay (the house's sheets of 2010, 2017 and 2018). That they grow on one of the four original vineyards along Felton Road was in no source read; cut, with the third trap that leant on it.
Bannockburn's Geographical Indication: registered on 1 February 2022 by the IPONZ register. That it was the first sub-region of Central Otago to be registered is in one blog only; cut.

changed.was: Bannockburn's terraces on the south side of the Kawarau were worked for gold in the nineteenth century, and its vineyards lie on the old sluicings. Vines came in the 1990s, when the owners of a handful of newly planted vineyards there, who called themselves the Gang of Four, chose to make wine together under one label rather than each alone. Mt Difficulty's first vintage was 1998. The growers' handshake held until 2004, when the company Mt Difficulty Wines was formed and the founding vineyards came into it. The house went on to bottle some of its vineyards apart: Pipeclay Terrace, from vines planted in 1996 on one of the four original vineyards along Felton Road, is released only in strong vintages, and Mansons Farm is made in small quantities. A second label, Roaring Meg, came to stand beside the first. In 2022 Bannockburn became a registered Geographical Indication of its own, the first sub-region of Central Otago to do so. For a sommelier, the Bannockburn Pinot Noir is the house's map of the sub-region in one bottle: fruit from many vineyards on gravel and clay, blended to show the place rather than one site.
changed.now: Bannockburn's terraces on the south side of the Kawarau were worked for gold in the nineteenth century, and its vineyards came to share the slopes with the old sluicings. In the 1990s the owners of a handful of newly planted vineyards there, who came to be known as the Gang of Four, chose to make wine together under one label rather than each alone. Mt Difficulty's first vintage was 1998. The growers' handshake held until 2004, when the company Mt Difficulty Wines was formed and most of the founding vineyards passed into it. The house went on to bottle some of its vineyards apart: Pipeclay Terrace, from vines planted in 1996 on coarse soils and heavy clay, is released only in strong vintages, and Mansons Farm is made in small quantities. A second label, Roaring Meg, came to stand beside the first. In 2022 Bannockburn became a registered Geographical Indication of its own, within Central Otago. For a sommelier, the Bannockburn Pinot Noir is the house's map of the sub-region in one bottle: fruit from several vineyards on gravel and clay, blended to show the place rather than one site.
changed.why: The vineyards sit beside the sluicings rather than on them; the growers came to be known as the Gang of Four; most, not all, founding vineyards passed into the company; the Felton Road placing of Pipeclay Terrace and the first registered sub-region were in no second source.

The making: hand picked, destemmed, a cold soak of five to seven days, indigenous yeasts, a maceration after fermentation, twenty two days on skins in 2021, twelve to fourteen months in French barriques, fifteen per cent new in 2010 and sixteen in 2021 (Vino Fino, Prince of Pinot, a profile of 2013, Wine.com). changed.was: In 1996, by the house's account, an Austrian born winemaker founded Quartz Reef with two partners, a Cromwell businessman and the farmer of Bendigo Station, who had marked out the slopes of Bendigo, on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, as new ground for Central Otago. The house took its name from the quartz reef that runs beneath the vineyard, by its own account the largest quartz deposit in New Zealand. The first vines went into Bendigo Station in 1998, and the first harvest came in 2001. Beside its Pinot Noir the house made sparkling wine by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in bottle, and became known for both. In 2007 it began to convert the vineyard to biodynamic farming, and in 2011 it gained Demeter certification, with its winery certified organic by BioGro. The estate bottles single blocks of the vineyard apart as its Single Ferment Pinot Noirs, beside the Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir. For a sommelier it is the warm end of Central Otago in a glass: dark, dense Pinot Noir from a slope that faces the sun.
changed.now: In 1996, by the house's account, an Austrian born winemaker who had first looked at the slopes of Bendigo, on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, in 1990 founded Quartz Reef with partners, among them the farmer of Bendigo Station. The house took its name from the quartz reef that runs beneath the vineyard, by its own account the largest quartz deposit in New Zealand. The first vines went into Bendigo Station in 1998, and the first harvest came in 2001. Beside its Pinot Noir the house made sparkling wine by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in bottle, and became known for both. In 2007 it began to convert the vineyard to biodynamic farming, and in 2011 it gained Demeter certification, with its winery certified organic by BioGro. The house also bottles one chosen parcel ferment of a vintage on its own, as its Single Ferment Pinot Noir, beside the Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir. For a sommelier it is the warm end of Central Otago in a glass: dark, dense Pinot Noir from a slope that faces the sun.
changed.why: The founding partners are the owner of Bendigo Station and others, no Cromwell businessman in any source read; the founder first looked at Bendigo in 1990; the Single Ferment is one chosen parcel ferment of a vintage.
